title: When Reduced Myocardial Strain Does Not Mean Myocardial Disease: The Emerging Role of Extrinsic Mechanical Determinants
content: Myocardial strain imaging has become an established tool for detecting subtle abnormalities in cardiac mechanics, and reduced strain is frequently interpreted as evidence of subclinical myocardial dysfunction. However, myocardial deformation reflects not only intrinsic myocardial properties but also the mechanical environment in which the heart operates. Emerging evidence suggests that extracardiac factors, particularly thoracic geometry and reduced antero-posterior (A–P) thoracic dimensions, may substantially influence global and regional strain even in individuals without overt structural heart disease. This narrative review examines the evidence supporting an extrinsically mediated myocardial deformation phenotype across different anatomical and physiological models, including pectus excavatum, mitral valve prolapse, healthy pregnancy, and obesity. A recurring feature is the preferential impairment of basal and, to a lesser extent, mid-ventricular deformation with relative preservation of apical mechanics, potentially generating a mechanical phenocopy of relative apical sparing. These abnormalities may reflect true mechanical constraint, measurement-related effects, or their combination, while intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms may coexist. Thoracic morphometry may therefore provide valuable context when unexpectedly reduced strain is encountered despite preserved conventional cardiac structure and function. The A–P thoracic diameter can be readily measured from the parasternal long-axis view, while the modified Haller index provides a more comprehensive, radiation-free characterization of thoracic conformation. Rather than equating abnormal strain with abnormal myocardium, myocardial deformation should be interpreted within a multiparametric and mechanistic framework integrating regional strain distribution, conventional cardiac findings, clinical probability, and the mechanical environment surrounding the heart. Accounting for these factors may improve diagnostic specificity and reduce the misclassification of extrinsically mediated strain abnormalities as subclinical myocardial disease.
